findings.title: Webhook secret comparison is not timing-safe and fails open when env vars are unset
findings.body: The webhook secret is compared with `!==` (non-constant-time, enabling timing attacks) and, more importantly, when `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` is unset the comparison becomes `header !== undefined`. If the attacker sends a request without the configured header, `req.headers[...]` is `undefined`, so `undefined !== undefined` is false and the check passes — the endpoint is then only protected by `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED`, which is truthy whenever both env vars are set... but note `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` is computed as `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, so if the secret is unset the feature flag is falsy and the endpoint returns 403. However, if `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` is set to an empty string (as in the shipped `.env.example`: `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET=""`), the flag is falsy too. The real risk: if an operator sets `CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` and `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` but the header name env var (`CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME`) is misconfigured or the secret is an empty string while the flag logic changes, any request without that header passes authentication. Additionally, `req.headers[...]` is `string | string[] | undefined`; comparing an array to a string with `!==` always passes for array-valued headers, and the value is never validated to be a string. Use a constant-time comparison (e.g. `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on hashed buffers) and explicitly reject when either env var is missing or empty.

findings.title: Unhandled Zod parse error returns a 500 with a stack-trace-bearing error instead of a 400
findings.body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throws a `ZodError` on invalid input. Because the handler does not catch it, Next.js returns a 500 and the raw Zod error (including the received payload shape) leaks to the caller. The endpoint should use `safeParse` and return a 400 with a generic message. The same applies to the `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` on line 57, which throws on malformed/undecryptable payloads, producing an unhandled 500.

findings.title: Decryption uses an empty-string key fallback and stores attacker-controlled JSON verbatim as the credential key
findings.body: `symmetricDecrypt(reqBody.keys, process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY || "")` silently falls back to an empty key. Depending on the implementation of `symmetricDecrypt` in `@calcom/lib/crypto`, an empty key may either throw or — worse — decrypt with a predictable key, letting an attacker who knows the code forge `keys` payloads. The handler must verify `CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` is set (and of the expected length) before decrypting and return 500/403 otherwise. Additionally, the decrypted `keys` value is `JSON.parse`d with no schema validation and written directly into `prisma.credential.key` (lines 78 and 85). A valid webhook caller (or anyone if the secret check is bypassed) can store arbitrary JSON — including a `refresh_token`/`access_token` of their choosing for any user and any app — which is then used by the calendar/video services to act against third-party APIs. The decrypted payload should be validated against a per-app credential schema before persisting.

findings.title: findFirst-then-update/create race allows duplicate credentials and lost updates
findings.body: The handler does `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })` and then either `update` or `create` based on the result. Two concurrent webhook calls for the same user/app both see no credential and both `create`, producing duplicate credentials for the same user+app (the schema does not enforce uniqueness on `(userId, appId)` — other callbacks in this codebase, e.g. zoomvideo/webex/tandem, explicitly `deleteMany` existing credentials first, confirming duplicates are possible). Concurrent updates can also overwrite each other. The write should be atomic — e.g. a transaction, or `upsert` on a unique constraint, or `updateMany`/`create` guarded by a transaction with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` semantics.

findings.title: Endpoint does not restrict HTTP method or content type
findings.body: The handler responds to any HTTP method (POST, GET, PUT, ...) and never checks `req.method`. A GET request with a query-string body would still be parsed by Next.js into `req.body` for some content types, and more importantly there is no method gate, so the endpoint's behavior is not constrained to the documented webhook POST. It should return 405 for non-POST methods. Relatedly, `req.body` may be a string if the content type is not JSON, which would make the Zod parse fail with a 500 (see the parse finding).

findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema uses invalid zod index-signature syntax and will not validate as intended
findings.body: The schema is written as `z.object({ access_token: z.string(), [z.string().toString()]: z.number(), [z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional() })`. Computed keys with zod schemas are not valid index signatures — zod index signatures must be created with `z.record(...)` or `.catchall(...)`. As written, zod will treat these computed properties as literal key names (the stringified schema objects) rather than catch-alls, so `minimumTokenResponseSchema.safeParse(response)` will strip/reject almost every real token response (any response containing `expires_in`, `refresh_token`, `token_type`, etc. will fail or be stripped), causing `parseRefreshTokenResponse` to throw "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned" for every synced refresh. The intent (require `access_token`, allow arbitrary extra fields) should be expressed as `z.object({ access_token: z.string() }).passthrough()` (or `.catchall(z.unknown())`).

findings.title: Missing refresh_token is silently replaced with the literal string "refresh_token"
findings.body: When the parsed token response has no `refresh_token`, the code sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"` — the literal string. This placeholder is then merged into the stored credential (e.g. office365calendar `o365AuthCredentials = { ...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data }`, zoom `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token`). On the next refresh, the service will send `refresh_token=refresh_token` to the provider, which will fail with `invalid_grant`, permanently breaking the credential instead of preserving the previous refresh token. The correct behavior when a provider omits `refresh_token` (common — many providers only return it on the first consent) is to keep the existing refresh token from the stored credential, not to fabricate one.

findings.title: Function returns a Zod SafeParseResult but callers treat it inconsistently (some read `.data`, some read `.success`)
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the whole `SafeParseResult` object. Callers use it inconsistently: `googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` line 97 does `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema)` and passes the SafeParseResult (not `.data`) to `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })` — persisting `{ success: true, data: {...} }` instead of the credential object, corrupting the stored credential. `salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts` line 90-94 correctly checks `.success`, and `office365calendar` line 263-264 uses `tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data`. The function should either return the parsed data directly (throwing on failure, which it already does) or all callers must be audited; returning the raw SafeParseResult invites exactly this class of bug.

findings.title: Credential sync endpoint is called without authentication, TLS validation is not enforced, and the response is trusted blindly
findings.body: When `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` is set, `refreshOAuthTokens` POSTs `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` to that endpoint with no authentication header, no signature, and no verification that the response actually corresponds to the requested user/app. Any party who can reach the Cal.com instance can point `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` (or an attacker who can influence env) at a server they control and have Cal.com store arbitrary `access_token`/`refresh_token` values into users' credentials — and conversely, the sync endpoint receives a list of which users use which apps. The request should carry a shared secret (e.g. `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`) and the response should be validated (schema + user binding) before being persisted. Also, the returned `Response` is passed to callers that call `.json()`/`.data` on it without checking `response.ok`, so a 4xx/5xx from the sync endpoint yields `undefined` tokens that are then written into credentials (see googlecalendar: `token.access_token` would throw, but hubspot/zoho write `tokenInfo.data` which would be an error body).

findings.title: Type mismatch: function returns a fetch Response in one branch and the provider's parsed body in the other
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens` returns `response` (a `Response` object) when syncing, but returns `await refreshFunction()` — which for most callers is the provider's parsed body or an axios response — in the normal path. Callers handle this inconsistently: `googlecalendar` does `const token = res?.data` (works for the googleapis `res` shape but for a fetch `Response`, `.data` is `undefined`, so `token.access_token` throws and the credential is marked invalid); `hubspot` assigns the result to `HubspotToken` and reads `.expiresIn`/`.accessToken` directly (a `Response` has neither, so `hubspotRefreshToken.expiryDate = Math.round(Date.now() + undefined * 1000)` = NaN and `setAccessToken(undefined)`); `zoho-bigin`/`zohocrm` read `tokenInfo.data` (undefined on a `Response`). The abstraction leaks two incompatible shapes; the function should normalize (e.g. always return the parsed JSON body) so every caller works in both modes.

findings.title: Synced refresh response is read as `res?.data` but refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response, so `token` is undefined and the credential update throws
findings.body: In `refreshAccessToken`, `const res = await refreshOAuthTokens(...)` then `const token = res?.data`. In the normal (non-sync) path `res` is `fetchTokens.res` (a GaxiosResponse, which has `.data`) — fine. But in the credential-sync path `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the raw `fetch` `Response` object, which has no `.data` property, so `token` is `undefined` and `token.access_token` throws a TypeError. The catch block then treats any error message other than "invalid_grant" by returning the stale `myGoogleAuth`, so the token is never refreshed and every subsequent API call fails with 401 until the credential is manually fixed. The response must be normalized (e.g. `await res.json()` when it is a `Response`) before reading `.data`.

findings.title: Stored credential key is replaced with the Zod SafeParseResult wrapper object instead of the parsed data
findings.body: `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema);` — `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns a `SafeParseResult` (`{ success, data }`), not the parsed value. This object is then passed to `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`, persisting `{ success: true, data: { ...tokens } }` as the credential key. On the next load, `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` in `googleAuth` will fail because the stored shape no longer matches, breaking the integration. It must be `parseRefreshTokenResponse(...).data` (and since the helper already throws on failure, `.data` is safe).

findings.title: parseRefreshTokenResponse already throws on invalid responses; the subsequent `.success` check is dead code and the merge can still persist a placeholder refresh_token
findings.body: `const tokenResponse = parseRefreshTokenResponse(responseJson, refreshTokenResponseSchema);` — the helper throws `"Invalid refreshed tokens were returned"` when parsing fails, so `tokenResponse.success` is always `true` here and the `tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data` guard is dead. More importantly, when the provider omits `refresh_token`, the helper injects the literal string `"refresh_token"` (see parseRefreshTokenResponse finding), and line 264 merges that into `o365AuthCredentials`, overwriting the real refresh token and permanently breaking future refreshes. The merge should preserve the existing `refresh_token` when the response doesn't include one.

findings.title: handleErrorsJson is called on the value returned by refreshOAuthTokens, which may be a parsed body rather than a Response
findings.body: `const responseJson = await handleErrorsJson(response);` assumes `response` is a fetch `Response`. In the sync path `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a `Response` (ok), but in the normal path it returns the result of the inner fetch — which here is also a `Response`, so this works — however the type contract of `refreshOAuthTokens` is `any` and other callers pass axios responses. If the contract is normalized to "parsed body" (as recommended in the refreshOAuthTokens finding), this call site breaks. The two paths must be reconciled so `handleErrorsJson` always receives a `Response`.

findings.title: Salesforce getClient now refreshes the token on every instantiation and overwrites the stored credential, and prisma is not imported
findings.body: The diff adds a full token-refresh block inside `getClient` (lines 75-99) that runs on every service construction — i.e. on every calendar operation — POSTing to Salesforce with the stored `refresh_token` and then `prisma.credential.update(...)`. Two problems: (1) `prisma` is used at line 96 but is never imported in this file (no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"` in the shown content), which is a compile/runtime error (`ReferenceError: prisma is not defined`) the first time any Salesforce calendar operation runs; (2) unconditionally refreshing on every `getClient` call discards the access-token caching/expiry logic that previously lived in the jsforce connection, causing an extra token request per operation and — because Salesforce rotates refresh tokens — can invalidate the stored refresh token if the update races with another concurrent operation. The refresh should happen only when the stored access token is expired, and `prisma` must be imported.

findings.title: Refreshed Salesforce credential is persisted without the original refresh_token when the response omits it, and without expiry_date
findings.body: Line 98 writes `key: { ...accessTokenParsed.data, refresh_token: credentialKey.refresh_token }`. `accessTokenParsed.data` comes from `parseRefreshTokenResponse`, which (a) injects the literal string `"refresh_token"` when the field is absent — here it is then overwritten with the real one, so that specific issue is mitigated — but (b) the `salesforceTokenSchema` has no `expires_in`/`expiry_date` field, so the stored credential never records when the new access token expires. The jsforce connection is constructed with `accessToken: credentialKey.access_token` (the OLD token, line 106) rather than the freshly fetched `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`, so the very first API call after a refresh uses a stale access token and fails with 401. The new access token must be used for the connection.

findings.title: Synced refresh response is passed to handleErrorsJson which expects a Response; expiry_date becomes NaN when syncing
findings.body: `const responseBody = await handleErrorsJson<ITokenResponse>(response);` — in the sync path `response` is a fetch `Response` (fine), but the code then computes `responseBody.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + (responseBody?.expires_in || 0) * 1000)`. The credential-sync contract (per `parseRefreshTokenResponse` and the PR description) is that the sync endpoint returns only the access token and an expiry timestamp, not `expires_in`. So `expires_in` is undefined, `expiry_date` becomes `Date.now()`, and `isExpired` (line 56, `expiryDate < Math.round(+new Date())`) immediately treats the fresh token as expired, causing an infinite refresh loop on every API call. The adapter must handle the sync response shape (absolute expiry) distinctly from the Microsoft token shape (relative `expires_in`).

findings.title: HubSpot refresh treats the refreshOAuthTokens return value as a HubspotToken, but in sync mode it is a fetch Response — expiryDate becomes NaN and the credential is corrupted
findings.body: `const hubspotRefreshToken: HubspotToken = await refreshOAuthTokens(...)` then `hubspotRefreshToken.expiryDate = Math.round(Date.now() + hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn * 1000)`. In the normal path the inner function returns the HubSpot SDK token object (has `expiresIn`), but in the credential-sync path `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a `fetch` `Response` object, which has no `expiresIn` — so `expiryDate` is `NaN`, `hubspotRefreshToken.accessToken` is `undefined`, and the credential is updated with `key: { ...Response-ish garbage }` (line 198), destroying the stored HubSpot credential. `hubspotClient.setAccessToken(undefined)` then breaks all subsequent calls. The sync response must be parsed (`await response.json()`) and mapped to the HubspotToken shape before use.

findings.title: zoho-bigin passes credentialId (a number) as the userId argument to refreshOAuthTokens
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens(fn, "zoho-bigin", credentialId)` — the third parameter of `refreshOAuthTokens` is `userId: number | null`, but the call site passes `credentialId` (the credential's primary key), not `credential.userId`. In sync mode the request to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` will therefore send `calcomUserId=<credentialId>`, which is the wrong identifier — the self-hoster's app store keys credentials by Cal.com user id, so the sync endpoint will look up (or create) tokens for a non-existent user and return an error/empty payload, breaking token refresh for every zoho-bigin user. The call must pass `credential.userId` (the `CredentialPayload` is available in `refreshAccessToken`'s closure via the class, but the method signature only receives `credentialId` and `credentialKey`; the method should also receive the credential or its userId).

findings.title: Token refresh result is used without checking HTTP status; axios errors and sync-mode Response objects are both mishandled
findings.body: `const tokenInfo = await refreshOAuthTokens(async () => await axios.post(...), ...)` then `if (!tokenInfo.data.error)`. In the normal path `tokenInfo` is an axios response (`.data` is the body — ok), but axios throws on non-2xx by default so the `else` branch logging `tokenInfo.data` is only reachable for 2xx responses containing an `error` field. In the sync path `tokenInfo` is a `Response` and `tokenInfo.data` is `undefined`, so `!tokenInfo.data.error` throws a TypeError (`Cannot read properties of undefined`) which is uncaught in `refreshAccessToken` and propagates to `getToken`, failing the whole calendar operation. The response must be normalized and its HTTP status checked.

findings.title: Zoho CRM refresh swallows all errors and leaves this.accessToken stale/undefined, then API calls proceed with an invalid token
findings.body: `refreshAccessToken` wraps everything in try/catch and on error only does `this.log.error(e)` — it does not rethrow, does not invalidate the credential, and does not set `this.accessToken`. `getToken` resolves successfully regardless, so `createEvent`/`updateEvent`/`deleteEvent` proceed to call the Zoho API with an empty or stale `this.accessToken`, producing confusing 401/NO_AUTH errors instead of a clear "credential invalid" signal. Additionally, in sync mode `zohoCrmTokenInfo` is a `Response` and `zohoCrmTokenInfo.data` is `undefined`, so `!zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error` throws inside the try and is swallowed by the same catch. The refresh must surface failures (or mark the credential invalid) rather than silently continuing.

findings.title: Lark refresh passes the fetch Response to handleLarkError which expects a Response in normal mode but the sync path also returns a Response — however the normal path previously returned a Response too; the real issue is handleLarkError is not applied consistently and errors are not surfaced
findings.body: `const resp = await refreshOAuthTokens(async () => await fetch(...), "lark-calendar", credential.userId)` then `const data = await handleLarkError<RefreshTokenResp>(resp, this.log)`. In the normal path `resp` is the `fetch` `Response` (same as before the change — ok). In the sync path `resp` is also a `Response` — ok by luck. But `handleLarkError` presumably throws on non-OK Lark responses; in sync mode a non-200 from the sync endpoint (e.g. 404 for unknown user) will be interpreted as a Lark API error and its body parsed as `RefreshTokenResp`, yielding `data.data.refresh_token === undefined`, which is then written into the credential (lines 91-96), wiping the user's Lark tokens. The sync response must be validated (ok status + expected shape) before its fields are persisted.

findings.title: Webex refresh passes the refreshOAuthTokens result to handleWebexResponse, which clones/reads it as a Response; in sync mode the body shape differs and expiry_date is never set from the sync payload
findings.body: `const responseBody = await handleWebexResponse(response, credential.id);` — `handleWebexResponse` (line 270) expects a fetch `Response` and returns `responseClone.json()`. In the normal path `response` is a `Response` (ok). In the sync path it is also a `Response` (ok), but the sync endpoint returns only `{ access_token, expiry_date }` (per the PR contract), which does not match `webexRefreshedTokenSchema` (requires `scope`, `token_type`, `refresh_token`, `refresh_token_expires_in`). `parsedToken.success` will therefore be false and the adapter rejects with "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned" — meaning Webex token refresh is permanently broken whenever credential syncing is enabled. The sync response must be mapped onto the webex token shape (preserving the existing refresh token and computing expiry) instead of being validated against the provider schema.

findings.title: Zoom refresh validates the sync endpoint response against the Zoom provider schema, which the sync payload does not satisfy
findings.body: `const parsedToken = parseRefreshTokenResponse(responseBody, zoomRefreshedTokenSchema);` — when credential syncing is enabled, `parseRefreshTokenResponse` uses `minimumTokenResponseSchema` (only requires `access_token`), so `parsedToken.data` will contain only the fields the sync endpoint returned (e.g. `access_token` and an expiry). But lines 119-122 then unconditionally read `newTokens.refresh_token` and `newTokens.expires_in` — both `undefined` for a sync response — so `key.refresh_token` is set to `undefined` (wiping the stored refresh token) and `key.expiry_date` becomes `NaN`, permanently breaking the Zoom credential. The code must preserve the existing `refresh_token` and derive `expiry_date` from the sync payload's absolute expiry when present.

findings.title: handleZoomResponse is called on the refreshOAuthTokens result, which in sync mode is a Response but in normal mode is also a Response; however the sync body lacks Zoom's error field so invalid_grant handling is bypassed
findings.body: `const responseBody = await handleZoomResponse(response, credential.id);` — `handleZoomResponse` throws on non-OK responses and returns the parsed JSON. In sync mode, if the sync endpoint returns 200 with an error payload or a non-JSON body, `responseClone.json()` may throw or return an unexpected shape; the subsequent `if (responseBody.error)` check (line 98) assumes the Zoom error shape. A sync endpoint that returns `{ "error": "user_not_found" }` with 200 would be treated as a Zoom `invalid_grant` only if the string matches; otherwise it falls through to schema validation and rejects with a generic error, and the credential is never invalidated even though the user's tokens are gone. The sync path needs explicit status/shape validation.

findings.title: APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is a string-or-undefined value, not a boolean, and is truthy for an empty-string secret
findings.body: `export const APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED = process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY;` — this evaluates to `string | undefined`, not `boolean`. It is used in boolean contexts (`if (!APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED)`), which works, but the exported name and type imply a boolean and the value can be the empty string `""` (falsy, ok) or the secret string itself (truthy). More subtly, the flag does not include `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`, so `refreshOAuthTokens`/`parseRefreshTokenResponse` check `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` — meaning the webhook endpoint is enabled whenever the secret+key are set even if no sync endpoint is configured, which is presumably intended, but the flag should be an explicit boolean (`!!(...)`) and the webhook handler should additionally verify that the encryption key is non-empty before decrypting (see the app-credential.ts finding about the `|| ""` fallback).

findings.title: New credentials created by the webhook are not marked with any indication they are externally managed, and team credentials are not supported
findings.body: The webhook always creates/updates a credential with `userId: reqBody.userId` and never sets `teamId`. Self-hosters syncing credentials for users who belong to teams will have the credential attached to the user rather than the team, so team event types that resolve credentials by `teamId` will not see the synced credential. Conversely, a webhook caller can attach a credential to any user id (the endpoint trusts `userId` after only checking the user exists), which is by design for this feature but means the endpoint is a full credential-write primitive for arbitrary users — combined with the weak secret check, this is a significant privilege. At minimum the created credential should be validated against the app's expected key schema (see earlier finding) and the behavior for team-owned apps should be documented/handled.

findings.title: Sync request sends credentials lookup parameters as URLSearchParams without a Content-Type header or any authentication
findings.body: The POST body is `new URLSearchParams({ calcomUserId, appSlug })` but no `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded` header is set (fetch sets it automatically for URLSearchParams bodies in modern runtimes, so this is mostly fine), and — more importantly — no authentication or shared secret is sent, so the sync endpoint cannot verify the caller is really this Cal.com instance (see the security finding). Also `appSlug` values passed by callers are inconsistent: googlecalendar passes `"google-calendar"`, office365video passes `"msteams"`, zoom passes `"zoomvideo"` — the sync endpoint must know this exact mapping; the PR description does not document the canonical slug list, which will cause silent mismatches for self-hosters.

findings.title: Unrelated hardcoded redirect URI change bundled into the rename commit
findings.body: The diff changes `const redirectUri = WEBAPP_URL + `/api/integrations/${appConfig.slug}/callback`` to the literal ``WEBAPP_URL + `/api/integrations/zoho-bigin/callback` ``. If `appConfig.slug` is not exactly `"zoho-bigin"` this changes the OAuth redirect URI and breaks the Zoho Bigin install flow (the redirect URI must match the one registered in the Zoho console). This change is unrelated to the credential-sync feature and should be reverted or justified.

findings.title: parseRefreshTokenResponse accepts `any` response and an unused schema parameter in sync mode
findings.body: The signature is `(response: any, schema: z.ZodTypeAny)`. In sync mode the `schema` argument is completely ignored (only `minimumTokenResponseSchema` is used), so callers pass provider-specific schemas that are silently discarded — meaning a sync endpoint returning extra/malformed fields is accepted as long as `access_token` is a string. The `any` type also disables type checking at every call site. The function should type the response as `unknown` and, in sync mode, still validate the minimal shape strictly (and ideally require an expiry field, since the whole point of the sync contract is to return token + expiry).

findings.title: appStoreMetadata lookup uses the DB app slug but the credential is written with appMetadata.slug — mismatch for apps whose metadata slug differs from the DB slug
findings.body: `const appMetadata = appStoreMetadata[app.slug as keyof typeof appStoreMetadata];` then the credential is created/updated with `appId: appMetadata.slug`. If `appStoreMetadata`'s key differs from `appMetadata.slug` (the lookup key vs the inner slug), the credential's `appId` will not match the `app.slug` that was validated to exist, and downstream credential resolution (which filters by `appId`) will not find it. The code should assert `appMetadata.slug === app.slug` or use `app.slug` consistently for the credential write.

findings.title: New env vars added to globalEnv include secrets that should not be listed as build-time env for all packages
findings.body: `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, `CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`, and `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME` were added to `globalEnv`. `globalEnv` in turbo affects cache hashing for every task in every package; listing server-only secrets there is not itself a leak (turbo does not print values), but it means builds of unrelated packages (website, ai, embed) will be invalidated when these secrets rotate and implies they are needed at build time for those packages, which they are not. More importantly, the web app's build env list (`@calcom/web#build` `env` array, lines 27-38) was NOT updated to include these variables, so production builds may not have them available at runtime in some deployment setups that rely on the turbo env allowlist. The web build env should include the four new variables (at least the ones read at runtime: `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME`, `CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`).

findings.title: Comment says to generate the webhook secret with `openssl rand -base64 32` but the encryption key comment says 24 bytes; the webhook secret has no length requirement and 32 is fine, but the two comments are inconsistent about which key is which
findings.body: The `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` comment says `openssl rand -base64 32` (44 chars, ~256 bits — fine for a shared secret) while `CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` says "must be 32 bytes for AES256" and `openssl rand -base64 24` (24 bytes = 192 bits, which is AES-192, not AES-256; 32 bytes needs `openssl rand -base64 32` or `openssl rand 32 | base64`). The encryption key comment is wrong: base64 of 24 random bytes is 24 bytes of key material = AES-192, not AES-256 as claimed. If `symmetricDecrypt` requires a 32-byte key, self-hosters following the comment will get a key of the wrong length. The comment should say `openssl rand -base64 32` for a 32-byte (AES-256) key, matching the existing `CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY` guidance at line 90.

findings.title: Team-owned credentials (userId null) silently fall back to the provider refresh path even when syncing is enabled, causing inconsistent behavior
findings.body: `if (APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT && userId)` — when `userId` is null (team credential), the function takes the `else` branch and calls `refreshFunction()`, i.e. it refreshes directly against the provider using the stored refresh token. But the entire premise of the feature (per the PR description) is that the self-hoster's app store is the source of truth and the Cal.com instance may not even have valid client secrets for the provider. For team credentials the refresh will fail (or worse, succeed against a provider the self-hoster has decommissioned), and the two code paths diverge. The function should either support team credentials in the sync call (e.g. pass `teamId`) or explicitly throw/log when syncing is enabled but the credential is team-owned, rather than silently falling back.

findings.title: refreshOAuthTokens is called with credential.userId which may be null for team credentials, silently disabling sync for team Google calendars
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens(fn, "google-calendar", credential.userId)` — `credential.userId` is `number | null`. For team-owned Google Calendar credentials `userId` is null, so the sync branch is skipped and the code falls back to refreshing directly against Google with the stored refresh token. For self-hosters using this feature, team credentials will not be synced and will break once the self-hoster rotates/decommissions the Google OAuth client. This should be surfaced (log/throw) rather than silently falling back, consistent with the refreshOAuthTokens finding.
